annotations.text:
1 · The couch bar
Tap the faces — they work on this artboard. Shows that everyone seated is part-way through come first, then ones only some of you are on.
Every card carries the two-part badge: the service on the left, the profile name to pick once you are there on the right.

2 · Finding it
Search is the whole add flow. Each result shows the same service-and-profile badge, so you can see where it will be filed before you tap.
The profile shown is the default you marked for that service. Tap through and you can change it.

3 · Adding it
Who is watching comes from the couch bar. Service comes from the search result. Profile is the default marked for that service on screen 6. Starting episode defaults to the beginning.
The dashed + next to the profile chips adds a new profile without leaving the sheet.

4 · The show
One position, yours. Bump it an episode at a time, or mark a whole season done in one tap when you have been watching without opening the app.
Watched-with is a tag list, not four separate progress counters — the app never claims to know where anyone else is.
The dashed row is the reserved spot for 'leaving the service', which we are not building yet.

5 · Two ways to demote
Not in the mood: half height, dimmed, no artwork, and it comes back on its own after a set time.
Decided not to finish: the smallest row on the screen, still searchable, stays down until you undo it.
Both drop the profile badge on purpose — that is part of taking less space.

6 · Profiles setup
One screen for the profile names as each service actually spells them. Netflix has four, Apple TV+ has two, Prime has one.
Profiles are not linked to people. One per service is marked as the default, and that is the only thing the marking does — it is what the add screen starts on.
The first profile you add to a service becomes its default, so this screen never has to be filled in up front.
Two other directions, deliberately left as rough sketches. Direction A is the one built out on the Screens page. Tell me which parts of B or C you want and I will fold them in.

1 . Ideas
Three sections, ordered by how much guessing each one does.
Ready tonight does none: it is your own wishlist, crossed with the services you pay for, filtered to the people on the couch. If this section has anything in it, the rest hardly matters.
Stalled does none either. It is your own started shows that have not moved, offered as a decision rather than a nudge.
Only the third section is a guess, and its heading names the show whose taste it borrowed.

2 . Why this one
Every suggestion can be opened to see its reasoning, and the reasoning is in plain sentences citing shows by name.
The screen also argues against itself. If you shelved something similar, that is listed, because a suggestion you already rejected the shape of is worth knowing about before you commit three seasons.
Not for us teaches it. Ask me later pushes it out ninety days.

3 . What it uses
Each signal is named, counted, and switchable. The counts come from the real library, so the screen doubles as a summary of what you have recorded.
The second half says what it never reads. That list matters more than the first: the app has no login to any streaming service and cannot get one, which is exactly why its suggestions are worse than Netflix's and also why they are only about you.
Shows you dropped are kept, not forgotten, so you can undo a no.

4 . Before it knows you
A new library has nothing to reason from, and the screen says so instead of inventing something.
It still fills the screen honestly. Ready tonight works from day one, because a wishlist entry plus a service you pay for needs no history at all. Popular on what you pay for is generic and labelled generic.
The counter gives a reason to mark old shows as finished, which is the fastest way to make the rest of this useful.
